chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: The target full-scale industrial WWTP was located in Shanghai, China, with a designed daily influent capacity of 40,000 m 3 d − 1 , using a typical A/O treatment process. It was responsible for the treatment of wastewater from a wide variety of companies in an industrial park, as well as a negligible amount of domestic wastewater produced in the park (Fig. 1 ). The received industrial wastewater was divided into five parallel process lines, denoted as Lines A to E, each being equipped with its own equalization, anoxic, aeration and secondary sedimentation tank. The effluent from secondary sedimentation tank was then compiled into four dissolved air flotation tanks, and further treated by a V-form filter, an ozone-contact tank and a biofilter consecutively, before discharge into the sea. chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

chunks.citation: Ge, HQ et al. (2011). Temperature phased anaerobic digestion increases apparent hydrolysis rate for waste activated sludge. WATER RES.
chunks.text: Anaerobic digestion is a biological decomposition process used to treat, stabilise, and reduce the quantities of organic wastes prior to disposal or beneficial re-use. Anaerobic digestion has been used extensively in municipal wastewater treatment to stabilise primary sludge and activated sludge. Over the past decade, municipal wastewater treatment processes have adapted to meet reduced discharge limits on the effluent nitrogen concentration. Process adaptations include the removal of primary settlings and primary sludge streams; and increased retention times for biological nutrient removal (BNR) processes, resulting in increased sludge age. Increased sludge age results in waste activated sludge with inherently low degradability, as inert materials in the influent, as well inert decay products accumulate in the activated sludge (Gossett and Belser, 1982) . Adaptations of modern wastewater treatment processes have introduced new challenges for anaerobic digestion, as poor degradability of activated sludge requires long digester retention times, higher mixing costs, and also results in poor gas production. Incorporating a pre-treatment into anaerobic treatment may enhance the sludge digestion by accelerating hydrolysis, which is generally accepted as the rate-limiting step in anaerobic digestion.

The drying kinetics increased as temperature was higher, and pellet diameter and relative humidity were lower. Temperature had the greatest influence on the drying kinetics (in both the constant and falling rate periods), followed by the effect of pellet diameter. The drying kinetics were affected in a moderate way by the relative humidity in the constant rate period and part of the falling rate period. The effective diffusivities increased from 7.81 Â 10 À8 to 1.97 Â 10 À7 m 2 /s by increasing the temperature from 40 to 80 C, leading to an activation energy of 23 kJ/mol. These values are typical from those found for wastewater sludge. chunks.text: The secondary biological treatment consists of two carrousel-shaped biological reactors with suspended biomass, equipped with two horizontal aerators, which include nitrogen removal. Regarding the sludge line, a fraction of the solids settled in the secondary settler is purged to the sludge thickener. Previously to the band filter, the sludge passes through a homogenizer to be mixed with cationic polyelectrolyte and further dewatered in the band filter prior being stored in a silo. Calafell WWTP was built on 1994 to treat the wastewaters of the municipalities of Calafell and Bellveí and designed for 70,000 population equivalent with a maximum flow of 12,000 m 3 /day. After a primary treatment, wastewater is treated in two activated sludge reactors with extended aeration including nitrogen removal, followed by the secondary settler. From these units, the treated wastewater is directly discharged to the submarine sewage. Some differences are observed in the operation of the plant between winter and summer seasons due to fluctuations on the population and changes on the influent composition. A coagulation-flocculation treatment, only operated during summer, receives the wastewater after the screening step.

chunks.text: As shown in Fig. 4 , the process boundary starts with the primary treatment process removing large floating particles and coarse solids. The grit removal step removes sand, gravel, dust and similar suspended solids. Oil skimmers scoop off oil residues (Wahlberg et al., 2005) . The secondary treatment step, biological treatment, uses activated sludge, microorganisms and microbial aggregates to reduce the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD) and suspended solids. In the aeration tanks, return activated sludge (RAS) from the clarifiers is used to decompose organic matter. Clarifiers also produce surplus activated sludge (SAS). SAS is sent to the sludge treatment process line. Up to 85% of BOD and total suspended solids can be removed after the completion of the secondary treatment process (Hsu et al., 2014) . The wastewater is then treated to the tertiary level using disc filters, ultraviolet (UV) filtration and chlorine disinfection. The amount of sludge generated from tertiary treatment is insignificant compared to that generated from secondary treatment (FAO, 2020). Sludge treatment aims to reduce the sludge volume by thickening, stabilization, conditioning, and dewatering.

chunks.text: An equalization tank was designed to maintain airflow and homogenize the incoming  wastewater, with a maximum volume of 30,000 m 3 and a depth of 4 m. In the biological step, the MBR bioreactor, as a prominent innovation in wastewater treatment, was designed with a total membrane surface area of 4200 m 2 and a porosity of cake layer equal to 0.15 m 2 . This design facilitates the degradation of both organic and inorganic substances, reduces sludge production, and produces high-quality effluent. Moreover, the tank volume was set at 9740 m 2 , and the backwash frequency and flow rate were assumed to be 30 s and 2000 m 3 /d, respectively. Then, the RO technology was implemented to enhance and complete the wastewater treatment process. The RO membranes, characterized by their small pore size, effectively reject molecules and ions, resulting in purified water. The RO system contained four vessels with a membrane area per element of 35 m 2 /element. The assumed recovery rate for the RO system was 60 %, meaning that 60 % of the feed water was treated and converted into purified water.
